wrong: Identify the make and model of the vehicle
Skid marks show braking and motion. Make and model come from paint chips, parts or tire tread impressions.
Estimate the time the collision occurred
Skid marks do not show the time of the crash; witnesses, CCTV or records do.
Find the driver's identity
Skid marks show how the vehicle moved, not who was driving it.
Examining paint transfer to match vehicles
Paint transfer links vehicles to a collision; it does not show how fast they were going.
Examining tire tread to identify the brand
Tread pattern analysis identifies the tire, not the vehicle's speed.
Checking brake lights for damage
Lamp examination shows whether lights were on at impact, not the speed.
Accidental burning and property damage
Accidental fires are not arson; arson requires willful burning with criminal intent.
Burning of property owned by another
Ownership is not the key element; even burning one's own property can be arson under PD 1613. What matters is willful burning with intent.
Burning caused by lightning
Natural fires involve no human intent and are not arson.
Ranking of officers in the investigation
That is the command structure. Chain of custody tracks who handled the evidence, when and why.
Order in which witnesses testify in court
The order of witnesses is a trial matter. Chain of custody documents how evidence was handled.
List of suspects in the case
A suspect list is not chain of custody, which records each transfer of the evidence.
Large objects that link a suspect to the scene
Size matters here: trace evidence is small, like hair, fibers, glass or soil.
Statements taken from eyewitnesses
That is testimonial evidence, not trace evidence.
Weapons recovered from the suspect
Weapons are physical evidence, but not trace evidence, which is minute material transferred by contact.
Fingerprints lifted at the scene
Fingerprints are physical evidence. Testimonial evidence comes from what witnesses say.
Documents seized during a search
Documents are documentary evidence, not testimonial evidence.
DNA from blood stains
DNA is physical (biological) evidence, not testimony.
Statement made against one's own interest
That is a declaration against interest. A dying declaration is made under the belief that death is imminent.
Written will made before the person dies
A will disposes of property; it is not a statement about the cause of death.
Statement made at the time of a startling event
That is part of the res gestae. A dying declaration requires belief that death is imminent.
Open questioning of possible witnesses
That is interviewing. Surveillance watches suspects without their knowledge.
Questioning a suspect in custody
That is interrogation, not surveillance.
Formal arrest of a suspect
Arrest takes the suspect into custody; surveillance observes without them knowing.
Officer working under a false identity
That is an undercover agent. An informant is a person, usually a civilian, who gives information to the police.
Person who saw the crime and testifies
That is an eyewitness. An informant gives information to the police and often never testifies.
Officer who receives and records tips
That is the handler, not the informant.
Searching in parallel lanes in one direction
That is the strip or line search. The grid search runs the strip search twice, at right angles.
Searching in circles from the center outward
That is the spiral search.
Dividing the area into pie-shaped sectors
That is the wheel or ray search.
Searching in parallel lanes across the area
That is the strip or line search.
Covering the area twice at right angles
That is the grid, or double strip, search.
Searching outward from the center along straight rays
That is the wheel or ray search, which moves along straight lines from the center, not in circles.
Dangerous Drugs Act of 1972
That is RA 6425, which RA 9165 repealed and replaced.
Comprehensive Firearms and Ammunition Regulation Act
That is RA 10591 of 2013.
Anti-Trafficking in Persons Act of 2003
That is RA 9208.
Using illegal drugs
That is drug use. Pushing is selling, trading or giving away drugs.
Manufacturing illegal drugs
That is manufacture, a separate offense under RA 9165.
Keeping drugs for one's own use
That is possession, a separate offense under RA 9165.
Occasional use of drugs at social events
That is recreational or occasional use; dependency is a compelling physical or psychological need for the drug.
Use of drugs under a doctor's prescription
Medical use under prescription is not dependency by itself.
First-time experimentation with drugs
Experimentation is trying a drug, not being dependent on it.
Heat, Fuel, and Oxygen only
That is the fire triangle. The tetrahedron adds the chemical chain reaction.
Heat, Fuel, Oxygen, and Water vapor
Water vapor is not an element of fire; the fourth side is the chemical chain reaction.
Heat, Smoke, Flame, and Chemical chain reaction
Smoke and flame are products of fire, not its elements.
Substance used to slow the spread of fire
That is a fire retardant, the opposite of an accelerant.
Substance used to put out a fire
That is an extinguishing agent.
Device used to detect smoke early
That is a smoke detector.
Materials treated to resist burning
That is fire-resistant material, the opposite of an accelerant.
Chemicals used to put out burning fuels
Those are extinguishing agents.
Residue left after a fire burns out
That is fire debris; it may contain traces of an accelerant, but it is not the accelerant.
Information, Interview, Investigation
Interviewing is part of interrogation, and investigation is the whole process; the third I is instrumentation.
Intelligence, Interview, Instrumentation
Intelligence and interview are not the first two I's; they are information and interrogation.
Information, Identification, Instrumentation
Identification is an aim of investigation, not one of its tools; the second I is interrogation.
Photograph the scene first
Photography comes early, but the cardinal rule is not to touch, alter or move anything until it is documented.
Interview witnesses at once
Witnesses are interviewed, but the cardinal rule protects the scene from being disturbed.
Call for backup
Backup may be needed, but the rule of the scene is not to touch anything.
Reason the criminal committed the crime
That is the motive, not the method.
Place where the crime was committed
That is the place of the crime, not the offender's method.
Time when the crime was committed
The time is a detail of the crime; modus operandi is the offender's method.
Full acknowledgment of guilt for the crime
That is a confession. An admission acknowledges facts that tend to prove guilt without admitting the crime itself.
Statement that the accused was elsewhere
That is an alibi.
Statement denying any part in the crime
That is a denial.
The body of the victim found at the scene
Corpus delicti means the body of the crime, the fact that a crime was committed, not literally the corpse.
Proof of who committed the crime
The identity of the offender is separate from corpus delicti.
The weapon used to commit the crime
A weapon may help prove it, but corpus delicti is the fact that the crime happened.
The corpse of the victim
Corpus delicti means the body of the crime, the fact that a crime was committed, not literally the corpse.
Testimony of the main eyewitness
Testimony may help prove it; corpus delicti is the fact that a crime was committed.
Identity of the person who did the crime
Who committed the crime is the identity of the offender, a separate matter from corpus delicti.
Random checking of possible suspects
Investigation is systematic, not random.
Trial of the accused before a judge
Trial is a court process that follows investigation.
Filing of charges by the prosecutor
Filing charges comes after the investigation.
Single criminal act by a group of friends
Organized crime is a continuing enterprise, not a single act.
Spontaneous violence committed by a crowd during civil unrest
That is mob or riot behavior, which has no lasting structure.
Loose group of youths committing petty crimes together
That describes a delinquent group without the hierarchy and continuity of organized crime.
Arresting a suspect caught in the act without a warrant
That is a warrantless arrest in flagrante delicto under Rule 113, Sec. 5. It does not involve inducing anyone.
Secretly recording a suspect's private phone conversations
That is wiretapping, which RA 4200 prohibits except under court authority.
Following a suspect secretly to learn their daily routine
That is surveillance, also called tailing or shadowing.
flag: The correct answer uses the US meaning. Under Philippine law (People v. Doria), inducing someone who had no intent to commit a crime is INSTIGATION, which is illegal; ENTRAPMENT is the lawful trapping of someone already willing. Question cdi_135 teaches the Philippine meaning, so the two contradict. Consider changing the correct answer to: Lawful means of catching a person already intending to commit a crime.

wrong: Open patrol of an assigned beat
Patrol is visible police presence; surveillance is covert.
Questioning residents door to door
That is canvassing, not surveillance.
Searching persons at a checkpoint
A checkpoint search is open and visible; surveillance is covert.
Following a suspect on foot
That is tailing or shadowing; casing studies a place before an operation.
Building a case file for prosecution
That is case preparation, not casing.
Interviewing neighbors after the crime
That is a neighborhood canvass.
Investigation using hidden cameras only
Hidden cameras are technical surveillance; undercover work means an officer takes on a false identity.
Patrol in uniform to deter crime
That is visible patrol, the opposite of undercover work.
Questioning of a suspect under custody
That is custodial interrogation.
Lawful trap for a willing offender
That is entrapment, which is allowed. In instigation the officer creates the criminal intent, so it is a defense.
Buy-bust operation against drug sellers
A buy-bust is a form of entrapment, which is lawful.
Tailing a suspect
That is surveillance, not inducement.
Engineering, Education, Emergency
Emergency response is not one of the 3 Es; the third is enforcement.
Enforcement, Evaluation, Economy
Evaluation and economy are not among the 3 Es.
Education, Enforcement, Environment
Environment is sometimes added as a later E, but the original three are engineering, education and enforcement.
Checking every vehicle at fixed checkpoints
That is blanket enforcement. Selective enforcement targets the violations and places that cause crashes.
Issuing warnings instead of tickets
That is a leniency policy, not selective enforcement.
Enforcing only on holidays and weekends
Selective enforcement is based on which violations and places cause accidents, not on the calendar.
Enforcing traffic laws on the road
That is traffic enforcement.
Teaching drivers and pedestrians road safety
That is traffic education.
Investigating the causes of road crashes
That is accident investigation.
